A collection of independent short practical situations from ordinary daily life.

shortItems.brief: At the supermarket, Lina checks how much money she has for groceries. Her basket costs more than she planned, so she puts a snack back and keeps the ingredients for tonight’s meal.

storyPattern.goal: Keep a grocery purchase within a personal spending limit
storyPattern.relationship: Shopper managing her own household spending
storyPattern.interaction: Compare the basket with the available budget and choose what to remove
storyPattern.outcome: Put back an extra snack and keep the planned meal ingredients

shortItems.brief: Two roommates review a grocery receipt, mark only the items for their shared dinner, and leave personal purchases unmarked.

storyPattern.goal: Separate shared meal costs from personal grocery purchases
storyPattern.relationship: Roommates sharing food and household expenses
storyPattern.interaction: Review a grocery receipt together and mark only the items for the shared dinner
storyPattern.outcome: The shared items are clearly marked while personal purchases remain separate

shortItems.brief: At lunchtime, a coworker asks which of two food bags is for the team meeting. Her coworker points out the note marked for the team, and she puts that bag by the meeting room.

storyPattern.goal: Get the correct food order to a team meeting
storyPattern.relationship: Coworkers coordinating a shared work task
storyPattern.interaction: Ask which lunch bag is for the meeting and use its note to identify it
storyPattern.outcome: Set the labeled order by the meeting room

shortItems.brief: Two housemates find their shared pantry shelf crowded. One suggests keeping the shared rice and oil together on the lower shelf; the other agrees, and they move them there.

storyPattern.goal: Make shared groceries easy to find in a crowded pantry
storyPattern.interaction: Suggest a shelf for shared staples and agree on where they belong
storyPattern.outcome: Move the shared rice and oil onto the agreed lower shelf

shortItems.brief: A worker asks her manager when she can take a short meal break because she has not eaten. The manager says she can go after handing work off to the next worker, so she puts her packed lunch in the staff fridge until then.

storyPattern.goal: Find a practical time to eat during a busy shift
storyPattern.relationship: Worker and manager coordinating a shift
storyPattern.interaction: The worker explains she needs a meal break, and they agree she can go after handing work off to the next worker
storyPattern.outcome: The worker keeps her packed lunch in the staff fridge until the agreed break

shortItems.brief: A shopper cannot find her usual yogurt, so she compares the package size and price of another plain variety and chooses one that suits her needs.

storyPattern.goal: Find a suitable substitute for an unavailable grocery item
storyPattern.interaction: Compare another plain variety by package size and price
storyPattern.outcome: Choose the alternative that meets her needs

shortItems.brief: At the supermarket, I compare a large bag of lentils with two small bags. The price per kilogram is lower for the large bag, and I have room to store it at home, so I choose it.

storyPattern.goal: Choose a suitable lentil package after comparing prices per kilogram
storyPattern.interaction: Compare the price per kilogram and consider available storage space at home
storyPattern.outcome: Choose the larger bag because its price per kilogram is lower and it fits at home

shortItems.brief: At a supermarket, a shopper looking for mild sauce asks her friend to hold a jar while she reads its ingredients. She spots chili and puts the jar back.

storyPattern.goal: Check whether a packaged food suits a flavor preference
storyPattern.interaction: Ask a friend to steady a jar while reading its ingredient list
storyPattern.outcome: Put the sauce back after spotting chili

shortItems.brief: Dana and Omer order takeaway together. They notice that they selected two large portions, although they want one portion to share. Dana asks for a smaller portion, and the counter worker changes the order before they pay.

storyPattern.goal: Order an amount of takeaway food that suits a shared meal
storyPattern.interaction: Notice an oversized portion and request a smaller one before paying
storyPattern.outcome: The counter worker updates the order to the smaller portion

shortItems.brief: At a deli counter, a customer asks for a small piece of cheese sliced thinly. The deli worker slices a little cheese, and the customer confirms that it is enough.

storyPattern.goal: Buy a suitable amount of deli food in a preferred form
storyPattern.interaction: State the desired quantity and ask for thin slices
storyPattern.outcome: Receive the small sliced portion and confirm it is enough

shortItems.brief: After dinner, Noa notices that the large container is not suitable for the leftover soup and suggests a small one. The housemates pour the soup into it and put it in the fridge.

storyPattern.goal: Store leftover food in a container that fits
storyPattern.interaction: Noa notices that the first container is not suitable and suggests a smaller one
storyPattern.outcome: Pour the soup into the smaller container and put it in the fridge

stories.brief: Yael shops for dinner, asks a grocery worker to compare soup-mix ingredient lists after the first alternative contains the ingredient she avoids, checks a different variety herself, chooses it, and plans to make soup with vegetables she has at home.

storyPattern.goal: Choose a packaged food that fits a stated ingredient preference
storyPattern.interaction: Compare ingredient lists after the first alternative proves unsuitable
storyPattern.outcome: Select a suitable product and adapt a meal around it

stories.brief: On Friday evening, Tamar makes tomato sauce for dinner while her partner Eyal prepares the rest of the meal. After tasting the sauce, Tamar says it is sharper than she expected and asks whether to add sugar. Eyal suggests grated carrot they already have; they add a little, taste again, and decide the sauce tastes right. They mix it with the pasta and put the remaining sauce in a small container for the next day.

storyPattern.goal: Make a shared meal taste right using ingredients already available
storyPattern.interaction: Taste, express a preference, and suggest a practical adjustment
storyPattern.outcome: Serve the balanced meal and store the remainder for later

stories.brief: At home, Noa and Gil notice that the salad expected with their shared takeaway order is missing. They decide not to return to the restaurant and make a quick salad from cucumbers and herbs they have at home while Noa sets out the food.

storyPattern.goal: Complete a shared takeaway meal when an expected side is absent
storyPattern.interaction: Check the order together, then compare returning to the restaurant with using available ingredients
storyPattern.outcome: Choose a homemade salad and serve dinner without making another trip

stories.brief: Employee Yael asks manager Amir to leave early for a family meal. They agree that Yael will finish the customer report and leave a short status note, while Amir takes the afternoon follow-up call and updates the customer.

storyPattern.goal: Arrange an early departure without leaving an urgent team responsibility unassigned
storyPattern.relationship: Employee and manager coordinating a work shift
storyPattern.interaction: Explain a time constraint, clarify the day's priority, and negotiate who will take over the later handoff
storyPattern.outcome: Yael finishes the report and leaves a clear note; Amir takes the customer call and updates the customer

stories.brief: Diva, an Israeli swimwear and underwear maker founded in 1942 by Czech-born Hirschthal brothers, grew from a two-person workshop into a Tel Aviv factory that employed more than 100 people and exported much of its production.

sources.title: The Swinging Sixties? – Israeli Fashion in the 60s
The Diva of swimwear

storyBeats: Diva opened in Tel Aviv in 1942 as a small sewing workshop established by the Hirschthal brothers, who had moved from Czechoslovakia to Palestine.
At first, two people worked at one machine, and the workshop made women’s underwear.
The Hirschthal family had experience sewing swimwear and women’s underwear in Czechoslovakia; Mrs. Hirschthal brought that trade knowledge to the designs.
An ISRAEL21c account says British officers stationed in Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria bought the workshop’s lingerie for their wives, helping the business grow.
Diva added bathing suits in 1948, six years after the workshop began making lingerie.
By the 1960s, the company had a large factory on Herzl Street in Tel Aviv and employed more than 100 workers.
The Film Archive account says about 80 percent of factory production was earmarked for export, including to Europe, South Africa, and South America.
Diva became an official sponsor of the annual Miss Israel pageant, whose contestants wore the company’s swimwear.
In a later company profile, the family’s designs included distinctive animal and flower prints made from its own designs rather than prints bought from suppliers.
By the time of that later profile, production had moved to Romania, while design, modeling, and sample-making were still done in Israel.

stories.brief: The Ora embroidery factory, established in Netanya in 1957 through a partnership between the Women’s League for Israel and the Ministry of Labour and Welfare, employed blind women making clothing, prayer shawls, maps, and other textile products.

sources.title: Cornerstone Ceremony for Ora House in Netanya
WLI’s Heritage
Collection of Textile Items Made in Israel

storyBeats: Ora was a weaving and textile workshop for blind women in Netanya, established through cooperation between the Women’s League for Israel and a government welfare ministry.
The Women’s League history says the workshop began in 1952 in a small building beside its Netanya compound; the Film Archive dates the factory’s official opening to 1957.
The welfare ministry gathered blind girls from across the country in Netanya for training; women trained in weaving formed the workshop’s first core group.
A 1955 newsreel record says the ministry trained 11 blind women in crafts, including weaving, typing, and Braille reading.
A sewing workshop operated beside the weaving workshop and used its fabrics to make women’s and children’s clothes, tablecloths, prayer shawls, and other Judaica.
Blind men later joined the weaving workshop, while the sewing workshop also employed new immigrants with disabilities.
The products were sold at a shop in the Women’s League compound, in stores around Israel, and abroad.
A catalog of Israeli textiles from the 1950s–60s records clothing labels reading “Ora – Hand-woven by Blind Women,” showing how the workshop identified its work on garments.
In the 1970s, the weaving factory and sewing workshop together employed more than 45 people across their manufacturing work, according to the Women’s League history.
The Women’s League history reports that the factory received the Kaplan Award; it also says the workshop aimed to help blind people earn a living through productive work.

stories.brief: A 1939 newsreel records the opening of a new market in Tel Aviv, offering a lead to the development of organized market shopping in the growing city.

sources.title: Opening of an Indoor Market on HaAliya Street in Tel Aviv
Local Plan 12-0008: HaAliya Market Complex
The Most Abandoned Buildings in Tel Aviv

storyBeats: HaAliya Market was built in southern Tel Aviv as part of a planned Central Market complex, between HaAliya, Wolfson, Chelno v, and what is now Matalon Street.
The complex included a retail market facing HaAliya Street and a wholesale market behind it, near Chelno v Street; the two served different stages of selling food.

The market answered a demand for a more organized place to buy food: Tel Aviv’s retail and wholesale trade had been spread through crowded streets and open areas, where goods were harder to inspect and manage.
The city’s technical department, led by engineer Yaakov Shifman (Ben-Sira), planned the retail building in the International Style, with indoor spaces arranged for market stalls.
The retail building used openings and varying ceiling heights to bring in daylight and air, and its drainage system was designed to help keep the market clean.

Stalls and fittings were planned for particular foods: the market had fish pools, cheese counters with glass ceilings to keep flies away, and special displays or cutting spaces for baked goods, meat, and poultry.
The wholesale market was arranged around a courtyard for unloading and loading carts or trucks; merchants had storage spaces, and an auction hall included seating for 200 people.

A newsreel documents the opening ceremony of the new indoor market on HaAliya Street, attended by acting Tel Aviv mayor Eliezer Shachटर, deputy mayor Simha Ehrlich, and Rabbi Yitzhak Yedidya Frankel, who affixed a mezuzah to the building.
The wholesale section struggled with limited storage as the number of businesses and suppliers grew; the city later added another floor to parts of the wholesale buildings.
Poultry slaughterhouses operated in the market’s basement. Their sanitation problems contributed to the eventual closure of the retail market in 1981, according to a later account of the site.

The city’s planning records describe the former retail and wholesale markets as separate parts of the complex; they also record that the retail building was added to the city’s preservation list, while plans called for the wholesale building to be demolished.

stories.brief: Diva, an Israeli swimwear and underwear maker founded in 1942 by Czech-born Hirschthal brothers, grew from a two-person workshop into a Tel Aviv factory that employed more than 100 people and exported much of its production.

sources.title: The Swinging Sixties? – Israeli Fashion in the 60s
The Diva of swimwear

storyBeats: Diva opened in Tel Aviv in 1942 as a small sewing workshop established by the Hirschthal brothers, who had moved from Czechoslovakia to Palestine.
At first, two people worked at one machine, and the workshop made women’s underwear.
The Hirschthal family had experience sewing swimwear and women’s underwear in Czechoslovakia; Mrs. Hirschthal brought that trade knowledge to the designs.
An ISRAEL21c account says British officers stationed in Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria bought the workshop’s lingerie for their wives, helping the business grow.
Diva added bathing suits in 1948, six years after the workshop began making lingerie.
By the 1960s, the company had a large factory on Herzl Street in Tel Aviv and employed more than 100 workers.
The Film Archive account says about 80 percent of factory production was earmarked for export, including to Europe, South Africa, and South America.
Diva became an official sponsor of the annual Miss Israel pageant, whose contestants wore the company’s swimwear.
In a later company profile, the family’s designs included distinctive animal and flower prints made from its own designs rather than prints bought from suppliers.
By the time of that later profile, production had moved to Romania, while design, modeling, and sample-making were still done in Israel.

stories.brief: The Ora embroidery factory, established in Netanya in 1957 through a partnership between the Women’s League for Israel and the Ministry of Labour and Welfare, employed blind women making clothing, prayer shawls, maps, and other textile products.

sources.title: Cornerstone Ceremony for Ora House in Netanya
WLI’s Heritage
Collection of Textile Items Made in Israel

storyBeats: Ora was a weaving and textile workshop for blind women in Netanya, established through cooperation between the Women’s League for Israel and a government welfare ministry.
The Women’s League history says the workshop began in 1952 in a small building beside its Netanya compound; the Film Archive dates the factory’s official opening to 1957.
The welfare ministry gathered blind girls from across the country in Netanya for training; women trained in weaving formed the workshop’s first core group.
A 1955 newsreel record says the ministry trained 11 blind women in crafts, including weaving, typing, and Braille reading.
A sewing workshop operated beside the weaving workshop and used its fabrics to make women’s and children’s clothes, tablecloths, prayer shawls, and other Judaica.
Blind men later joined the weaving workshop, while the sewing workshop also employed new immigrants with disabilities.
The products were sold at a shop in the Women’s League compound, in stores around Israel, and abroad.
A catalog of Israeli textiles from the 1950s–60s records clothing labels reading “Ora – Hand-woven by Blind Women,” showing how the workshop identified its work on garments.
In the 1970s, the weaving factory and sewing workshop together employed more than 45 people across their manufacturing work, according to the Women’s League history.
The Women’s League history reports that the factory received the Kaplan Award; it also says the workshop aimed to help blind people earn a living through productive work.

stories.brief: A 1939 newsreel records the opening of a new market in Tel Aviv, offering a lead to the development of organized market shopping in the growing city.

sources.title: Opening of an Indoor Market on HaAliya Street in Tel Aviv
Local Plan 12-0008: HaAliya Market Complex
The Most Abandoned Buildings in Tel Aviv

storyBeats: HaAliya Market was built in southern Tel Aviv as part of a planned Central Market complex, between HaAliya, Wolfson, Chelno v, and what is now Matalon Street.
The complex included a retail market facing HaAliya Street and a wholesale market behind it, near Chelno v Street; the two served different stages of selling food.

The market answered a demand for a more organized place to buy food: Tel Aviv’s retail and wholesale trade had been spread through crowded streets and open areas, where goods were harder to inspect and manage.
The city’s technical department, led by engineer Yaakov Shifman (Ben-Sira), planned the retail building in the International Style, with indoor spaces arranged for market stalls.
The retail building used openings and varying ceiling heights to bring in daylight and air, and its drainage system was designed to help keep the market clean.

Stalls and fittings were planned for particular foods: the market had fish pools, cheese counters with glass ceilings to keep flies away, and special displays or cutting spaces for baked goods, meat, and poultry.
The wholesale market was arranged around a courtyard for unloading and loading carts or trucks; merchants had storage spaces, and an auction hall included seating for 200 people.

A newsreel documents the opening ceremony of the new indoor market on HaAliya Street, attended by acting Tel Aviv mayor Eliezer Shachटर, deputy mayor Simha Ehrlich, and Rabbi Yitzhak Yedidya Frankel, who affixed a mezuzah to the building.
The wholesale section struggled with limited storage as the number of businesses and suppliers grew; the city later added another floor to parts of the wholesale buildings.
Poultry slaughterhouses operated in the market’s basement. Their sanitation problems contributed to the eventual closure of the retail market in 1981, according to a later account of the site.

The city’s planning records describe the former retail and wholesale markets as separate parts of the complex; they also record that the retail building was added to the city’s preservation list, while plans called for the wholesale building to be demolished.
